\section{Unbinned background subtraction by negative-weight injection} \label{app:negweight} Background subtraction in \S\ref{sec:method-algo} is the only step that uses analysis binning before final histogramming.
Each data event in reconstructed bin $b$ receives the purity weight $w_{\mathrm{pur}}(b)=\max(0,\,N_{\mathrm{data}}(b)-N_{\mathrm{bkg}}(b))/ N_{\mathrm{data}}(b)$.
Injecting background simulation on the measured side with negative weight gives a fully unbinned correction with the same bin-integrated estimand.
Its agreement with the binned correction is quantified on the 2D measurement below.

It is the continuous version of the purity weight recommended for nontrivial backgrounds in Ref.~\cite{Canelli:2025guide}, and the natural treatment for the larger backgrounds of the extended-fiducial analysis.
Every cross section and uncertainty quoted in this note uses the binned purity weight of \S\ref{sec:method-algo}, except the 2D result and its covariance and the 3D and 4D central values.

Refined negative-weight subtraction is used by configurations (d), (e) and (f) (\S\ref{sec:method-config}): (d) in the background-bias and generator-sized-change studies of \S\ref{sec:val-negweight}, (e), the joint-test estimator, in \S\S\ref{sec:val-departure}--\ref{sec:gbdt-model-dependence}, the generator tests (\S\ref{sec:joint5d}) and the 3D and 4D central values (\S\ref{sec:3d}), and (f) for the 2D result and its covariance (\S\ref{sec:results}).
Here negative-weight injection is an equivalence study and the natural extended-fiducial treatment; this appendix establishes no supported production path and changes no default.
Background treatment is entirely a choice of $\rho_1$: \begin{itemize} \item binned purity assigns every data event in reconstructed analysis bin $b$ the same scalar.
For $x\in b$, \begin{equation} \label{eq:negweight-purity} \rho_1^{\mathrm{pur}}(x) \;=\; D(x)\,w_{\mathrm{pur}}(b) \;=\; D(x)\,\max\!

\Big(0,\;1-\frac{B_{b}}{D_{b}}\Big), \end{equation} where $D$ is the data density, $B$ the POT-scaled background density, and $D_{b},B_{b}$ their bin masses; \item negative-weight injection appends reconstructed background-simulation events to the measured side with weight $-w_{\mathrm{bkg}}\,\times\,(\text{POT scale})$ and keeps data weights at $+1$, giving \begin{equation} \label{eq:negweight-continuous} \rho_1^{\mathrm{neg}}(x) \;=\; D(x)-B(x) \end{equation} pointwise, without analysis binning.
\end{itemize} Equations~\eqref{eq:negweight-purity} and \eqref{eq:negweight-continuous} differ as functions of $x$.
\paragraph{The floor.} Where $D-B<0$, binned purity floors the correction at zero through $\max(0,\cdot)$.
Clipped Stay-Positive refinement removes this pathology and recovers binned-purity agreement to a median $\nwSpMedian$ ($\nwSpWithin$ bins within \SI{5}{\percent}).
This clipped refinement is therefore what makes the unbinned subtraction robust across estimators, and it matters most for the larger, more structured backgrounds of the extended-fiducial analysis.

\subsection{Binned limit: exact reduction to the purity correction} \label{sec:negweight-binned} A step-1 classifier restricted to functions piecewise-constant on reconstructed analysis bins $\{b\}$ gives the population-level binned limit of the OmniFold/Richardson--Lucy correspondence in Refs.~\cite{Andreassen:2019cjw,Andreassen:2021zzk}.
Injecting background simulation at negative weight while keeping data at $+1$ gives $W_1=D(b)-B(b)$.
\end{equation} Purity gives exactly this reweight under the same sieve, since its class-1 weight $W_1=D(b)\,w_{\mathrm{pur}}(b)=\max(0,\,D(b)-B(b))$ equals $D(b)-B(b)$ on this domain.
At $D(b)=B(b)$, the infimum lies at $p\to0^+$ and $r(b)\to0$, again giving purity when the boundary is admitted.
Stay-Positive remains well behaved but can retain negative refined weights where the target density is genuinely negative.
The zero clip used here is therefore an additional analysis prescription chosen to match the physical purity floor.
The binned $D-B$ update, negative-weight classification of the measured side, and binned OmniFold/Richardson--Lucy correspondence already appear together in Ref.~\cite{Andreassen:2021zzk}.
The known target $(D-B)/S=\phi(x;0.3,1.1)/\phi(x;0,1)$ is smooth and positive.

A signed-weight gradient-boosted classifier recovers it with median \SI{\nwToyNeg}{\percent} relative error, matching binned purity's \SI{\nwToyPur}{\percent} and reproducing it bin-for-bin on the same problem.
Results are stable across classifier seeds ($\pm\SI{\nwToySeed}{\percent}$), with no numerical instability from negative weights.

\subsection{Which background treatment each production chain uses} \label{sec:negweight-footing} Agreement between the two subtractions does not make the choice between them arbitrary, and the production chains choose differently.

\paragraph{The standard \(N\)-dimensional chain uses purity.} The entire standard five-dimensional chain uses binned purity (\S\ref{sec:method-algo}): the central unfold, $169$ vertical-band unfolds, $18$ detector unfolds and $10$ endpoint unfolds of the re-selected lateral bands.
Its background treatment is positively identified, by different evidence for the existing unfolds and for current production.
For the existing endpoint unfolds, produced in July 2026, purity is established by elimination.

Neither of the two job scripts that could have produced them sets the driver's background-mode option (\texttt{-{}-bkg-mode}), so the driver ran with its default, purity; the driver announces its mode only on its negative-weight code paths, and the logs of these lateral-band unfolds contain the purity code path's signature line and no mode announcement.
The option and the announcements already existed when the files were produced, so the absence of an announcement is evidence of purity.
Current production fixes the background treatment in a configuration object that rejects every other mode.
The standard job script passes the option explicitly from that configuration rather than inheriting the default, and the value is written into the record of every endpoint unfold as it is produced.
This changes how the treatment is documented, not the physics: the background treatment of a future component can be read from the component itself rather than inferred from the absence of an option.
The standard chain uses purity by choice, on two grounds (Ref.~\cite{NoteRecords2026}, \texttt{oi6-oi8-oi126}).

First, mixing background treatments inside one covariance is worse than either consistent choice: inserting a lateral-band block built with negative-weight subtraction into a central and vertical set built with purity subtraction is a mismatch, not an upgrade.
The background treatment has been revisited in two dimensions: the closure test below is its result, and the 2D result and its covariance use the refined estimator.
For the five-dimensional central value, which still uses purity, the revisit is open.

\paragraph{A two-dimensional closure test with backgrounds.} Twenty pseudo-experiments at nominal truth (the truth model equals the prior), with background included and drawn as in the five-dimensional pseudo-experiments, were unfolded in two dimensions with the purity subtraction and with refined negative-weight subtraction (a 400-tree, 31-leaf refinement), both on the same pseudo-data.

The yardsticks are the statistical and total standard deviations, $\sigma_{\mathrm{stat}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}$, of the purity-based 2D covariance on its 205 reported cells (the quoted covariance when the test ran).

End-to-end tests on simulation show biases that are not included in their quoted uncertainty: when the simulated truth is changed by a test pattern of the size of a difference between generators, typical cells come back about \SI{10}{\percent} off and the highest-$W$ cells much more, which we read as the method's pull toward its starting simulation; and the background removal leaves a bias in some cells.
A follow-up study traced this remaining bias to an auxiliary classifier in the background removal that was too simple; with a larger one the same test passes at the unchanged truth.

The quoted five-quantity central values still use the original removal, with its bias of up to \SI{4}{\percent} in the highest-$W$ cells; the improved removal is used for the three- and four-quantity central values and for the test of five simulations below.

The same kind of test for the two-variable result puts the original and the improved removal more than one statistical standard deviation apart in 14 of its 205 cells, with the improved removal within half a statistical standard deviation of the truth in every cell, and that result now uses the improved removal.
And the hypotheses are defined only down to the fine grid: convergence as that grid is refined has not been shown, and the possible error from structure finer than it is not bounded.
The original version of PET reads only the hadronic recoil (the energy deposited by particles other than the muon), so it does not use the muon, even though the muon is needed to select the event.
No design or default was selected, and no PET uncertainty is used for any result.

The tests of that extension are this study's main result, for this implementation: a background-removal bias of up to \SI{4}{\percent} in some cells; a remaining bias under generator-sized changes of the truth, read as the method's pull toward its starting simulation; statistical error bars, of a variant of the method, that miscover at the tested truths; and a spread of about \SIrange{10}{13}{\percent} per cell over five tested starting simulations, which keeps every tested way of reporting a five-quantity measurement from meeting the \SI{10}{\percent} precision we adopted as a target, under the reporting study's prescription.

The rejections hold only under six stated conditions, in particular that the test has no uncertainty for the calorimeter's response to the hadronic recoil and that convergence as the fine grid defining the hypotheses is refined has not been shown; and the test gives no evidence that the five quantities together discriminate better than matched coarse projections.
